newsitem.title: UK: British gilts to outperform after 1997 election.
newsitem.headline: British gilts to outperform after 1997 election.

text.p: British government bonds missed the Europe-wide rally inspired by economic convergence in 1996 but now look set to outperform, once the general election is out of the way, analysts said.

"Gilts have just failed to shine because they haven't been part of the convergence story. But next year, the markets will be looking a bit more sensibly at fundamentals rather than EMU euphoria," said Kevin Adams, an analyst at BZW.
Short-term, analysts see more selling as the election looms and early 1997 economic data shows more vigorous growth.
But longer-term they say the gilt yield curve will flatten and the 10-year spread between gilts and German Bunds will narrow.
QUARTER ONE - EDGY ON INFLATION, ELECTIONS

Any sustained rally next year will depend on reduced political uncertainty, along with market confidence that interest rates will soon rise to stem inflationary pressures. But this may not happen until after the general election, which has to be held by May. The first quarter is set to be particularly edgy with markets concerned that Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke will be reluctant to tighten rates in the run-up to the polls.

"If, as we suspect, markets realise over the coming months that he is "behind the curve' in this respect -- that he is running too loose a policy -- then sterling is likely to depreciate significantly and the gilt market perform poorly," said Michael Dicks at Lehman Brothers.
As 1996 ends, the sterling futures market is discounting the view that official interest rates could rise as high as 6.75 percent compared with the present six percent.

Britain's underlying inflation is low by historical standards, rising 3.3 percent in the year to November, but there are fears that lively consumer spending will allow retailers to push prices higher.

BZW's Adams predicted that inflation jitters would help the 10 year gilt/Bund spread widen to more than 200 basis points from around 190 now. "In the near-term there must be a threat. We've flirted with 200 several times already." Andrew Seaman, fund manager at Guinness Flight, sees the spread peaking somewhat higher.
"It will peak somewhere over 200, 220 perhaps. A bad economic number would do that but that would be its limit."
The latest economic data clearly showed activity shifted up a gear in November. Retail sales rose a robust 0.7 percent in the month while unemployment plunged by 95,800 -- the largest fall on record.
A growing consensus of City forecasters said the data will make it very hard for Clarke to leave rates on hold when he meets with Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George on January 15.

But a small band of analysts predict that Clarke will try his best to leave interest rates unchanged during the final weeks before the election. The embattled ruling Conservatives are lagging Opposition Labour badly in opinion polls.
"We think he'll try and muddle through to the election," said Tom Rayner, gilts analyst at Societe Generale.
He also sees general nervousness surrounding a possible change-over of government taking its toll.

"I think the biggest risk is that there is no overall majority, that there is a hung parliament and they have to come to a political fudge.. that's the worst scenario and that's something you can't ever fully discount."
AFTER THE FIRST QUARTER - GILT/BUND SPREAD TO NARROW
But after the election things could change.
Not only will there be less reason to resist monetary tightening, but economic fundamentals will come to the fore and yield spreads between gilts and Bunds will look too generous.
BZW's Adams predicts a narrowing of rates from 200 to "something closer to 100" over the next 12 months.
Rayner at Societe Generale sees a fairly rapid narrowing to 160 from around 200 in the months after the election.
"We're looking for tightening of spreads, some considerable tightening after the election when we would have our political worries out of the way," he said.
Any narrowing beyond 160 will depend on inflation, and buoyant consumption and a tight labour market might prevent it.
And gilts could be caught in the crossfire if the European convergence starts to falter.

Guiness Flight's Seaman said while he saw the yield spread narrowing further in the year, disenchantment with peripheral European countries that may not make monetary union in 1999 would affect bond markets across Europe and thus gilts would be hit in absolute terms.
Weaker economic data, rather than the end of the election, will be the main spur for gilts, he said.

"The major catalyst for a stronger gilt market will be weaker economic data and that won't happen for a while," he said. Seaman expects a volatile year with the spread around 150 at the end of the year.
